b: "There are two tragedies in life. One is not to get your heart's desire. The other is to get it." —George Bernard Shaw
"Happiness cannot be pursued. You do not find happiness; happiness finds you. It is not an end in itself, but a by-product of other activities, often arriving when it is least expected." —Mick Brown
The second of the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism is that the root of all suffering is desire, which manifests in its extremes as craving and aversion.
Immediately there’s a paradox: Why would we get out of bed if we didn’t desire to get out of bed and “do something”?
So how do we learn to desire the right things and not perpetuate our own suffering?

Firstly, I never liked the word “right” because it’s moralistic, black-and-white, and implies a corresponding “wrong.” I prefer “propitious,” or favorable, likely to promote well-being. We all experience a range of emotions, and there are propitious tools that keep us at the higher end of our happiness range and unpropitious tools that keep us at the lower end. If this sounds familiar, it is because it is also the focus of positive psychology.

The problem is that growing up in our society, we are taught, or at least led, to desire things that do not lead to long-term well-being and happiness. Our system exploits our mind's desire for novelty, for more-better-different, so that we remain constantly unsatisfied and always wanting more and more and more. More is never enough, and instant gratification takes too long. That is the engine of our society. It’s designed to increase gross domestic product and other numbers on screens, not individual happiness.
The Buddhist Eightfold Path helps people design lives that mitigate suffering and thus increase long-term happiness. The Buddha suggests that we espouse the...
1. Most propitious view: an accurate understanding of the nature of reality (including how our minds, left to their own devices, chase more-better-different).
2. Most propitious intention: letting go of attachment, hatred, and harmful intent.
3. Most propitious speech: avoiding lies, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter, and let’s throw in gossip too. :-)
4. Most propitious action: avoiding killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
5. Most propitious livelihood: avoiding work that harms others, such as trading in weapons, living beings, intoxicants, or poisons.
6. Most propitious effort: releasing negative states of mind, preventing new ones, and sustaining positive ones.
7. Most propitious mindfulness: awareness of body, feelings, thoughts, and phenomena.
8. Most propitious concentration: cultivating focused attention.

The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path are the heart of Buddhism. For me, there is an overlap between positive psychology and Buddhism because both invite us to look beyond the quick pleasure of immediately attaining our desires and ask what supports a more satisfying and meaningful life. One approaches it from understanding and reducing suffering; the other studies the conditions and practices associated with well-being. Both provoke us to notice the difference between momentary gratification and what nourishes us over time.

Obviously, less propitious things to desire are the ones that feed our egos, such as a car or vacation chosen because it looks cool to other people, a job title that exists to impress our parents, or trying to accumulate followers on social media so that we can earn money by "influencing" them to buy certain things. Desiring these ego-gratifications feels good in the moment but ultimately causes suffering, because we try to cling to and/or repeat the ephemeral joy and try to avoid everything less than joyous. Instead, as with positive psychology, if we design a life full of thoughts, habits, practices, commitments, and behaviors that nourish us—such as secure intimate relationships, balance, equanimity, purposeful work, time to rejuvenate, time to learn new things, and inspiration from both natural beauty and human-created beauty such as music and art—then we are committing our attention to things that bode well for engendering long-term happiness.

In How to Survive Your Childhood Now That You’re an Adult, I employ the image of a beacon that a ship uses to guide itself to shore: If we wake each morning wishing that our tombstones will someday read “Beloved,” then we have a surprisingly practical way of choosing our activities for that day. Congruence is deciding who you should be and then having the tools—such as the Eightfold Path—to be that person, lest the ocean of possibilities toss and turn your ship willy-nilly in random directions.

And if you’re looking to earn bonus points, instead of letting your mind endlessly chase more-better-different, learn to desire what you already have. (Hint: This is also known as “gratitude.”) So take a few minutes to acknowledge that you have food to eat today, a roof over your head, and a few minutes to spend with another human being.
